situation (example wording): "How many murders were there in Chicago in 2024?" asked without choosing a data source
what the app does today: Auto mode guesses a source; when it is not confident it shows a list of sources to pick from. On a chosen tab, that tab's data answers, with a banner when another source fits much better.
proposed behavior: Answer from one source chosen by a fixed order of preference, and name the source in the answer. Ask only when two sources would give materially different answers and nothing in the question decides it.
exact default or choices offered: Order: hate crimes -> FBI Hate Crime file; homicide victim or offender details -> Homicide Reports; victim, offender, weapon, relationship, location or property details -> NIBRS; this year or recent months -> Current Trends; completed years, long history, clearance and police staffing -> Historical.
why: The same question can return different numbers from different sources. A fixed order makes answers repeatable, and naming the source lets the reader check it.

situation (example wording): "How many robberies were there in the US in 2015?" on NIBRS, when only part of the country reported to NIBRS that year
what the app does today: Adds up the agencies that reported, with a statement of how many agencies and how much population they cover, saying it is not an estimate.
proposed behavior: Answer with the reported total and the fixed sentence "These are reported NIBRS counts." When the reporting agencies cover less than a set share of the population, decline the national or state total and offer the FBI estimate from Historical instead.
exact default or choices offered: Proposed threshold: 80% of the population. Alternative offered: "US robberies in 2015, FBI national estimate (Historical)".
why: A total from agencies covering a third of the country reads like a national figure. The new answer format carries no coverage note beside the number, so a threshold has to do that work.
test cases: H1-H3 (national sentence); new cases to write

situation (example wording): "How did aggravated assaults change in Texas from 2018 to 2024?" (NIBRS; many agencies joined during those years)
what the app does today: Counts every agency that reported in each year, so agencies joining looks like crime rising. Consistent reporters only when the user asks.
proposed behavior: For a state or national trend across years, count only agencies that reported in every year shown, and say so in one fixed sentence. Count every agency only when the user asks.
exact default or choices offered: Default: agencies that reported in every year shown. On request: all reporting agencies.
why: Current Trends already works this way. Without it, NIBRS trends mostly measure agencies joining.

situation (example wording): "Top 20 cities by murder rate in 2024" where some cities reported only part of the year
what the app does today: Includes them, with their first and last reported month and a caveat that spans differ.
proposed behavior: Leave out agencies that did not report all 12 months, and state how many were left out (rankings of change already do this, frozen rule 7).
exact default or choices offered: Default: full-year reporters only, with "N agencies with fewer than 12 months were not ranked". On request: include them.
why: A city with 4 months of data ranks far too low on a count. Frozen rule 5 forbids filters the user did not ask for, so this needs Jeff's explicit decision: completeness is not size.
test cases: GC-065, GC-066, GC-067, GC-068, GC-069, GC-118 (rule 7); new cases to write

situation (example wording): "Which cities had the most murders?" with no year, when the latest year in the data is incomplete
what the app does today: Uses the latest year with any data, titled "(Partial)" when incomplete.
proposed behavior: Rank the latest complete year and name it. Rank a partial year only when the user asks for this year or year to date.
exact default or choices offered: Default: the latest year whose December is in the data.
why: A partial year ranks agencies by how many months they have reported so far.

situation (example wording): "Murders in Houston" (one figure, no period) and "murders in Houston over time" (a trend, no period)
what the app does today: Differs by tab: Current Trends uses every month it has; Historical every year; NIBRS the latest complete year (another NIBRS path uses the last 5 years); Homicide Reports every year since 1976; Hate Crime the last 10 years.
proposed behavior: One rule on every tab, with the period named in the answer: a single figure uses the latest complete year; a trend uses the last 10 complete years.
exact default or choices offered: Single figure: latest complete year. Trend: last 10 complete years, by year.
why: The same question should not cover 1 year on one tab and 50 on another.

situation (example wording): "Burglaries in Texas last year"
what the app does today: Current Trends: the latest full year in its data. NIBRS and Historical: the calendar year before today, declined if not in the data yet.
proposed behavior: Always the calendar year before today. If that year is not in the source yet, say so and offer the latest year it has as a button; never answer another year silently.
exact default or choices offered: In October 2026: 2025. Offer: the same question for the latest year available.
why: "Last year" has one everyday meaning; answering another year without saying so is a wrong answer.
test cases: adapter test (last year); new cases to write

situation (example wording): "Which large US city had the highest violent crime rate in 2023?"
what the app does today: Answered by whichever tab is open. Current Trends covers about 700 agencies; NIBRS its reporters; Historical (FBI annual data) the most.
proposed behavior: For a completed year, answer from Historical (the widest coverage). For the current year, from Current Trends, naming its sample.
exact default or choices offered: Completed year: Historical. Current year: Current Trends.
why: A national comparison should include as many cities as possible.

situation (example wording): "How many assaults in Phoenix in 2024?" (the word "assault" alone)
what the app does today: Current Trends counts aggravated assault only. NIBRS counts all assaults (aggravated, simple, intimidation). The pre-submit helper offers a choice.
proposed behavior: Count aggravated assault and say so. Count all assaults, or simple assault, only when asked.
exact default or choices offered: Default: aggravated assault. On request: all assaults; simple assault.
why: Aggravated assault is the FBI's violent-crime measure, and today the same word gives two different counts on two tabs.

situation (example wording): "How many homicides in Memphis in 2023?" on Homicide Reports and on NIBRS
what the app does today: NIBRS and Current Trends: homicide means murder. Homicide Reports: "homicide" means all homicide victims, "murder" means murder only.
proposed behavior: "Homicide" and "murder" both mean murder and non-negligent manslaughter on every tab. Negligent manslaughter and justifiable homicide only when asked ("all homicides").
exact default or choices offered: Default: murder and non-negligent manslaughter. On request: all homicide types.
why: One word should mean the same count on every tab.

situation (example wording): "How many theft victims in Ohio in 2024?" and "How many thefts in Ohio in 2024?"
what the app does today: NIBRS counts offenses either way and says property crimes are counted by offense. Current Trends declines any "victims" question.
proposed behavior: When the user says "victims", count victims (NIBRS records victims of property crimes too). When no unit is named, use the standard unit: victims for crimes against persons, offenses for property crimes.
exact default or choices offered: "Victims" -> victims. No unit named -> the standard unit.
why: The user named the unit; answering in another unit answers a different question.

situation (example wording): Any answer that used to carry a caveat ("reporting agencies only", coverage notes)
what the app does today: Many answers carry caveat sentences. Frozen rule 8 says caveats come with every answer.
proposed behavior: Answers carry only fixed, approved sentences (for example "These are reported NIBRS counts."), never free-written caveats. Each fixed sentence appears in every answer it applies to, which keeps rule 8.
exact default or choices offered: The approved sentences form a short list; adding one is Jeff's decision.
why: Jeff's rule of 28 October (no editorializing, no notes) and rule 8 (caveats every time) fit together only if caveats become a fixed list.

situation (example wording): An empty answer: no matching records, a true zero, missing reports, or something the source does not hold
what the app does today: Frozen rule 13 says which of four cases it is. The new answer format allows no notes beside numbers.
proposed behavior: Each of the four cases gets one fixed sentence. Empty cells stay blank and the sentence says why.
exact default or choices offered: Four sentences to approve: reported zero; the agency did not report; no records, which is not evidence of zero; not available in this source.
why: Keeps rule 13 inside the no-notes answer format.

situation (example wording): General rule: when does the app ask a clarifying question?
what the app does today: Several separate rules (bare "crime", shootings, place level, ambiguous place names), each with its own trigger.
proposed behavior: Ask only when materially different readings remain after the explicit wording, the conversation so far and the approved defaults in this table. Never ask about something a default here settles.
exact default or choices offered: One question at a time, with buttons; each button runs the whole original question with that choice filled in.
why: Professional apps ask rarely and for a reason; every unnecessary question costs the user a turn.

situation (example wording): "What is the safest city in America?" / "most dangerous city"
what the app does today: Declines: no agreed definition; asks the user to name an offense and a count or rate.
proposed behavior: Ask with buttons, then rank: violent crime rate, murder rate, or property crime rate.
exact default or choices offered: Choices: violent crime rate (first), murder rate, property crime rate. Year: latest complete.
why: The question is common and answerable once the measure is chosen; declining sends the user away.

situation (example wording): "Murders in Chicago from 1990 to 2024" asked on NIBRS, which has Chicago only for recent years
what the app does today: Each tab reads only its own data; no rule for a span only another source covers.
proposed behavior: Never join two sources in one series. Answer from the one source that covers the whole span (here Historical) and name it; if none does, answer the covered part and name the missing years (frozen rule 4).
exact default or choices offered: Source: the one covering the whole span; otherwise the covered years, with the gap named.
why: Sources count differently; a joined series shows jumps that are not real.

situation (example wording): "Robbery rate in Georgia in 2024" on NIBRS
what the app does today: Divides by the population of the agencies that reported (weighted by months reported), not the whole state.
proposed behavior: Keep today's rule, and say whose population in one fixed sentence: "per 100,000 residents of the reporting agencies".
exact default or choices offered: Denominator: population of the agencies counted.
why: Dividing partial counts by the whole state understates the rate.
test cases: N1 (rate rules); new cases to write

situation (example wording): "Which cities have the most police officers per resident?" (Historical staffing)
what the app does today: The model's instructions add a 50,000 population minimum, which frozen rule 5 forbids for other rankings.
proposed behavior: No population minimum unless the user gives one, as rule 5 says for every other ranking.
exact default or choices offered: Default: no minimum. The user can add one ("cities over 100,000").
why: One ranking rule everywhere; an unrequested filter changes the answer.

situation (example wording): "Crime in Las Vegas", where the city is policed by a combined city-county agency or by several agencies
what the app does today: A city name means that city's police department, without saying which agency.
proposed behavior: Keep the city's principal police agency, and name it in the answer as county answers already do (rule 10).
exact default or choices offered: Default: the city's principal police agency, named.
why: The reader should know whose numbers they are reading.

situation (example wording): "Top 10 cities by murders" where the 10th and 11th are tied
what the app does today: Cuts at 10. Some rankings break ties by agency code, others in no fixed order.
proposed behavior: Include every agency tied at the cutoff (the list may run past 10), ordered by name within the tie.
exact default or choices offered: Ties at the cutoff: all included.
why: Dropping one of two equal values is arbitrary and can change between runs.

situation (example wording): "Burglary clearance rate in Ohio in 2023" (Historical has agency and national clearance, not state)
what the app does today: Declined when the request is clearly a state.
proposed behavior: Decline the state figure and offer two buttons: the national clearance rate (Historical), or Ohio's cleared offenses from its NIBRS agencies.
exact default or choices offered: Alternatives: national figure; NIBRS figure for Ohio's reporting agencies.
why: Frozen rule 14: offer the nearest measure that genuinely exists.

situation (example wording): "Fentanyl seizures in Ohio"
what the app does today: NIBRS declines ("falls under broader narcotic categories") with no alternative.
proposed behavior: Decline and offer the category that contains it: synthetic narcotics (fentanyl and other synthetic opioids).
exact default or choices offered: Alternative: synthetic narcotics, same place and period.
why: Frozen rule 14: a nearest measure exists here.

situation (example wording): "Will crime go up next year?" or any forecast
what the app does today: No rule found.
proposed behavior: Decline: the data records past crime and cannot predict. Offer the recent trend for the same place and measure.
exact default or choices offered: Alternative: last 10 complete years for the place and measure.
why: A forecast is not in the data; a plain statement beats an improvised answer.

situation (example wording): "What happened in the shooting on Main Street last Friday?" or a named person
what the app does today: No rule found.
proposed behavior: Decline: the data has no names, addresses or case narratives. Offer the count of that offense for the city and month.
exact default or choices offered: Alternative: offense count, same city and month.
why: Incident details are in no source.

situation (example wording): The user clicks a button in a clarifying question
what the app does today: The button rewrites the word in question and keeps the rest. Some questions are asked once only; the place-level question repeats until answered.
proposed behavior: A button runs the original question with only that choice changed (place, period and filters kept), and the same question is never asked again in that conversation.
exact default or choices offered: Not applicable.
why: Re-asking, or dropping parts of the question after the user answered, feels broken.

situation (example wording): Follow-up "What about Dallas?" after a Houston question
what the app does today: Replaces the place; keeps the source, offense, filters, measure, grouping and period.
proposed behavior: Keep today's behavior.
exact default or choices offered: Not applicable.
why: It is what users expect.

situation (example wording): "Burglaries in Denver in 2027" (a year not yet in the data)
what the app does today: Declines and states the covered range; some tabs point to another source.
proposed behavior: Decline, state the latest month or year available, and offer it as a button. Never answer another year silently.
exact default or choices offered: Offer: the same question for the latest year available.
why: Rule 4 already requires stating the range; the button saves a retype.

situation (example wording): "How many cases were cleared because prosecution was declined?" and "How many were convicted?"
what the app does today: Answers police clearances; declines court outcomes.
proposed behavior: Keep.
exact default or choices offered: Not applicable.
why: Police clearance is in the data; court outcomes are not.

situation (example wording): "Crime in my neighborhood", a ZIP code or a police beat
what the app does today: Declined on every tab.

situation (example wording): "Murder rate for Black victims" or rates by age group
what the app does today: Declined; offers counts or shares.
proposed behavior: Rates only for places (city, state, nation); offer counts or shares by group.

situation (example wording): A series with missing years, or a period outside the data

situation (example wording): "Top 20 cities by murder rate"
what the app does today: No population minimum (one Historical instruction still adds one; see P18).
proposed behavior: No filter the user did not ask for: no population or count minimum. The number of rows is stated.

situation (example wording): "Murders this year" or any partial year
